title: LFU cache
sub: Buckets by frequency, LRU inside a bucket, and a minFreq that is never searched for
cards/0/title: The problem: least frequent, and on a tie least recent
cards/0/body:
LFU Cache (LeetCode #460, hard). A cache of capacity capacity with Get(key) and Put(key, value), both O(1) on average. When there is no room, evict the key that was used least often (least frequently used). If several keys tie, evict the one among them that was used least recently, as in LRU.

A key's count is the number of Get and Put calls on it since it was inserted. A new key starts at 1. An evicted key's count is forgotten: if it comes back, it starts at 1 again. Constraints: capacity ≤ 10⁴, keys ≤ 10⁵, up to 2·10⁵ calls.

The signals are the same as for LRU: “implement the class”, O(1) per operation, “evict the least …”. But the order is now two-level — by frequency first, by recency within a frequency — and a single list cannot hold it: a key with count 5 cannot simply be “moved to the front” when keys with count 9 may be ahead of it.
cards/1/q: Capacity 2: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Get(2), Get(1), Put(3, 3). Which key does Put(3, 3) evict?
cards/1/options/2: None: 3 does not fit and is not inserted
cards/1/options/3: Either one: their counts are equal
cards/1/explain: Keys 1 and 2 have two uses each — a frequency tie. Recency breaks it: key 2 was last touched by Get(2), key 1 later, by Get(1). Key 2 goes.
cards/1/wrong/1: Key 1 was touched last (Get(1) came after Get(2)), so it is the more recent of the two.
cards/1/wrong/2: A new key is always inserted: eviction makes room for it.
cards/1/wrong/3: A tie is not arbitrary: the statement says to evict the least recent of the tied keys.
cards/2/body:
Dictionary + (freq, tick). For each key store the value, the count and the timestamp of the last use. Get and Put are O(1), but eviction scans all keys for the smallest (freq, tick) pair: O(capacity). In the worst case that is 2·10⁵ · 10⁴ = 2·10⁹ operations.

SortedSet<(int freq, long tick, int key)>. Tuples compare field by field from left to right — exactly the LFU rule with recency as the tie-breaker. The victim is Min, O(log n); a use is Remove of the old tuple and Add of a new one, O(log n). An honest solution, name it — but not O(1), and every Add is a tree node on the heap.

A PriorityQueue heap. It looks natural: “take the lowest frequency”. But a key's priority changes on every use, and PriorityQueue cannot change a priority (collections unit). Lazy deletion — enqueue the key again and skip stale copies — bloats the heap: there are as many copies as there were uses.

What repeats: every eviction searches for the minimum from scratch, although between evictions frequencies only grow by 1.
cards/3/q: Why is PriorityQueue<int, (int freq, long tick)> a poor fit for LFU?
cards/3/options/0: A key's priority changes on every use, and it cannot change a priority — only enqueue copies
cards/3/options/2: Removing the minimum is O(n) in it
cards/3/options/3: It returns elements in insertion order
cards/3/explain: PriorityQueue is a heap without decrease-key, and finding an element in it takes a scan (Remove arrived only in .NET 9 and costs O(n)). Without a scan, the only way to update a key's frequency is lazy deletion: enqueue a copy with the new priority and skip the old one when it comes out. Every use adds a copy, so the heap grows with the number of calls, not with the capacity.
cards/3/wrong/1: Tuples compare field by field through Comparer<T>.Default — that works.
cards/3/wrong/2: Dequeue on a heap is O(log n). The trouble is updating a priority, not removing the minimum.
cards/3/wrong/3: It is a heap: it returns the minimum by priority, and equal priorities in arbitrary order.
cards/4/body:
Spread the keys over buckets: bucket f holds all keys that were used exactly f times. Inside a bucket is a list in recency order, the least recent first: that is an LRU for a single frequency. The dictionary map stores an entry per key: the value, the count freq and the node in its bucket's list.

A use (a Get, or a Put on an existing key): unlink the node from bucket f — O(1), it is in hand — and append it to bucket f + 1. Eviction: the first key of the bucket with the lowest frequency. To avoid searching for that bucket, keep a field minFreq.

minFreq changes in only two cases. A new key: minFreq = 1 — nothing is used less often than a new key. A use emptied bucket f and f was the lowest: minFreq = f + 1 — the key that left has just landed exactly there, and there is nothing below f. If a bucket above the lowest empties, minFreq stays. There are no other changes: a use moves one key up by one bucket, and an eviction is immediately followed by the insertion of a new key.

Without minFreq, eviction would look for a non-empty bucket by scanning frequencies from the bottom, and frequencies grow up to the number of calls — 2·10⁵. Invariant: minFreq is the number of the lowest non-empty bucket. Time is O(1) on average per operation, memory is O(capacity).
cards/4/flow/1: node: bucket f → end of f + 1
cards/4/flow/2: f empty and f == minFreq → minFreq++
cards/5/q: Assemble the move between buckets and the eviction.
cards/5/explain: Remove(e.node) is O(1) by node. Remove(e.freq) compiles (the list holds ints), but it removes by value, with a scan, and the wrong element. minFreq grows only when exactly the lowest bucket empties. The victim is the first key of bucket minFreq, and after the eviction a new key with count 1 is inserted, so minFreq = 1.
cards/6/task: Walk the trace of the LeetCode example: capacity 2. Buckets go by use count, the least recent key in a bucket is on the left. The rig will stop twice: on minFreq and on a tie.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Scan the buckets from the bottom to find a non-empty one
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Keep minFreq = 1 until the next put
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: get(3) moved key 3 from bucket 1 to bucket 2, and bucket 1 is now empty. minFreq was 1. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: Bucket 1 was the lowest and it emptied, and the key that left it landed in bucket 2 — so bucket 2 is non-empty and there is nothing below it. One comparison and an increment. Keeping 1 is wrong: the next eviction would reach into an empty bucket.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Both: the whole bucket is freed
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: put(4, 4): the cache is full, minFreq = 2, bucket 2 holds keys 1 and 3. Whom does the code evict?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: The frequencies are equal, so recency breaks the tie. Keys are appended to a bucket: 1 after get(1), 3 later, after get(3). The first in the list is the least recent: victims.First, key 1. Exactly one key is evicted — to make room for one new key.
cards/7/q: Capacity 2: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Get(2), Get(2), Put(3, 3) — and Put throws a NullReferenceException. Tap the buggy line.
cards/7/explain: minFreq grows whenever any bucket empties, not only the lowest one. The second Get(2) empties bucket 2 while minFreq = 1 and key 1 is still in bucket 1 — and minFreq becomes 2. Put(3, 3) takes buckets[2], an empty list: First == null, and First.Value throws. The condition needs && minFreq == e.freq.
cards/8/title: Why it is O(1), and what it costs
cards/8/body:
Why O(1). Every operation is a dictionary lookup (O(1) on average), at most two list operations by node (O(1)) and one comparison for minFreq. Not a single loop over keys or buckets: everything we used to search for is now kept — the list keeps the order inside a bucket, minFreq keeps the lowest bucket.

Memory. Per key: an Entry object (32 bytes on 64-bit) and a LinkedListNode<int> (48 bytes), plus one LinkedList object per frequency. On a use the node moves between buckets by itself, without a new allocation: after Remove it is unlinked and can be inserted again.

Empty buckets. In the code above an emptied bucket stays in the buckets dictionary. Frequencies grow up to the number of calls, and the dictionary can pile up thousands of empty lists. You can remove a bucket when it empties — but then the list is created again the next time a key reaches that frequency. In an interview it is enough to name the trade-off and pick one.
cards/8/deep:
Buckets as a list, no frequency dictionary. The buckets can themselves form a doubly linked list ordered by frequency: each bucket knows its neighbours and its frequency. A use moves the key into the next bucket on the right — if its frequency is f + 1 — or creates that bucket between the current one and its neighbour. An emptied bucket is removed at once, and minFreq is just the first bucket. The same shape solves All O(1) Data Structure (#432): inc, dec, getMaxKey and getMinKey in O(1).

Without allocations. Just like LRU on indices: keys, values, frequencies and the prev/next links live in arrays of capacity plus sentinels; a bucket is a “head, tail” pair in an array indexed by frequency or in a freq → bucket number dictionary. After the constructor, not a single object.

Can the count overflow? An int is 2.1·10⁹ uses of one key. The problem has 2·10⁵ calls, and in a long-lived service counts age anyway (next card), so they never get near the limit.
cards/9/title: When LFU is worse than LRU
cards/9/body:
LFU remembers the past: a key that was used a lot an hour ago stays on its count even if it is no longer needed. That causes two problems.

1. Stale keys. The player has left the first biome: its sounds and textures racked up thousands of uses and now never get evicted, while the new biome's assets fight over what is left of the cache.
2. Newcomers go first. A new key starts at 1 and is evicted before everyone else, even if it will be needed constantly: it never gets the chance to build up a count.

LRU reacts to a change of pattern at once: whatever is not touched goes. That is why games default to LRU, and LFU pays off when popularity is stable: frequent lookups of reference data, shared UI resources.

The cure is aging. Every N operations, or on a level change, all counts are halved — old merit fades. That is O(n) once every N operations, cheap when amortized. Another option is a hybrid: a small LRU window for new keys, and only keys that have proven their frequency get into the main part. In an interview, naming both problems and aging is enough.
cards/10/q: A sound cache uses LFU. After a biome change the old biome's sounds are never evicted, while the new biome's sounds keep getting evicted and reloaded. What helps? Select all.
cards/10/options/0: Aging: halve all counts on a biome change
cards/10/options/1: Switch to LRU: sound popularity changes with the biome
cards/10/options/2: Double the capacity — and the problem is gone for good
cards/10/options/3: Reset minFreq to 0 on a biome change
cards/10/options/4: Switch to a SortedSet by (freq, tick)
cards/10/explain: The problem is stale counts. Aging makes them fade, and LRU ignores past merit altogether — a good fit when popularity changes. A bigger capacity only delays the problem until the next biome. minFreq is the number of the lowest non-empty bucket, and setting it to 0 breaks the invariant. A SortedSet changes the cost of operations, not the eviction rule.
cards/11/q: You are solving LFU Cache out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: what counts as a use, how a frequency tie is broken, what happens to an evicted key's count
cards/11/items/1: Name the honest solution: a SortedSet by (freq, tick) — O(log n) per operation
cards/11/items/2: The idea: buckets by frequency, recency order inside a bucket, plus a minFreq field
cards/11/items/3: Explain why minFreq is never searched for: it is reset to 1 or grows by 1
cards/11/items/4: Write Get, Put and Touch, then walk an example with a tie
cards/11/items/5: Complexity: O(1) on average per operation, O(capacity) memory
cards/11/items/6: Say when LFU is worse than LRU and what aging is
cards/11/explain: The tie and use rules come before the code: the structure depends on them. O(log n) is the baseline and a fallback. What interviewers want to hear on this hard problem is the minFreq argument: why it is enough and why it needs no search.
cards/12/q: Match each event in the LFU cache with what the code does.
cards/12/pairs/0/1: From bucket f to the end of bucket f + 1
cards/12/pairs/3/1: The first in the bucket is the least recent
cards/12/pairs/4/0: Old keys hang on by their count
